title: Many Experiments, Few Repetitions, Unpaired Data, and Sparse Effects: Is Causal Inference Possible?
claim: Prior estimator's error stays flat as the number of environments grows; ours keeps improving with more environments and repetitions.
layout: 2 side-by-side heatmaps, shared axes and colorbar, left-to-right comparison
description: Two side-by-side heatmaps share one color bar on the right. The left panel is titled 'two-sample IV (TS-IV)' and the right panel 'SplitUP (analytic)'. The x-axis is the number of environments m, log-spaced from 50 to 3200. The y-axis is observations per environment (τ = n/m), with values 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32. Color shows mean absolute error of the estimated coefficients. It runs from orange-brown for high error (about 1) through yellow to green for low error (about 0.01). The left panel is striped horizontally. Error depends only on observations per environment and does not drop as m grows. The right panel has a gradient from orange at the bottom-left to deep green at the top-right. Error falls as m and τ increase. The eye goes first to the contrast between the flat left panel and the green corner on the right.

Our proposed estimator SplitUP (right) outperforms existing methods (left) if the number m of experimental conditions increases. Indeed, we prove identifiability in the setting m →∞in Section 3. In Section 4, we show that unlike existing estimators (such as TS-IV on the left), SplitUP is consistent as n, m →∞and n/m →r ∈(0, ∞).
abstract: We study the problem of estimating causal effects under hidden confounding in the following unpaired data setting: we observe some covariates $X$ and an outcome $Y$ under different experimental conditions (environments) but do not observe them jointly; we either observe $X$ or $Y$. Under appropriate regularity conditions, the problem can be cast as an instrumental variable (IV) regression with the environment acting as a (possibly high-dimensional) instrument. When there are many environments but only a few observations per environment, standard two-sample IV estimators fail to be consistent. We propose a GMM-type estimator based on cross-fold sample splitting of the instrument-covariate sample and prove that it is consistent as the number of environments grows but the sample size per environment remains constant. We further extend the method to sparse causal effects via $\ell_1$-regularized estimation and post-selection refitting.
